page: Microsoft Azure D64pds_v6 is a general-purpose virtual machine built on Microsoft's ARM-based Neoverse-N2 processor architecture. It offers 64 dedicated physical cores without simultaneous multithreading, providing 64 vCPUs running at a clock speed of 3.4 GHz. Memory allocation is balanced at 256.0 GB of RAM, adhering to a 1:4 vCPU-to-memory ratio (4.0 GB per core). Cache configurations include 64 KB of L1 data cache, 1.0 MB of L2 cache, and a large shared 128 MB L3 cache. In addition to standard compute and memory provisions, the instance integrates 3780 GB of attached local NVMe SSD storage. It operates without discrete GPUs.

Benchmark data displays strong multithreaded compute and memory throughput. The server scores in the top 10% for multi-core stress-ng performance (132,407.53) and multi-core Geekbench (23,662.0), supported by dedicated non-hyperthreaded physical cores. Software compilation in Geekbench places in the top tier at 65,067.0. Large-block memory bandwidth benchmarks fall into the top tier, measuring 467.26 GB/sec for uncached reads and 174.46 GB/sec for writes. PassMark database operations and multi-threaded bzip3 decompression both reach top-tier rankings.

While parallel throughput is substantial, single-threaded metrics reflect average performance. Geekbench single-core and stress-ng single-core results land in the middle 50% band. The ARM architecture lacks x86-specific vector instruction sets like AVX-512 or AMX, though hardware AES encryption is present. The architecture provides high resource density per core, yielding qualitative cost efficiency for multi-threaded workloads, though applications requiring maximum per-thread IPC or specific x86 vector extensions may observe architectural limitations.

The instance is well configured for parallelized enterprise environments, including distributed caching, large-scale databases, software compilation clusters, web serving fleets, and data preprocessing pipelines. The integrated 3780 GB NVMe SSD suits workloads that require high-capacity, low-latency scratch storage or temporary database partitions.
